title: Senior's toolkit: measure, then make it Pythonic
summary: timeit, cProfile and py-spy to find the slow part, itertools to fix it, and ruff to keep the idioms.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: measure, then make it Pythonic
steps.body: Experienced developers do not guess which line is slow: they measure, change one thing, and measure again. Then a linter keeps the codebase idiomatic so reviews can talk about design instead of style.

toolkit.what: Time a small snippet properly: it repeats it many times and reports the best average, so noise does not fool you.
flags: code run once before timing (imports, test data)
how many runs per measurement (default: chosen for you)
toolkit.example: python -m timeit -s "xs = list(range(10_000)); s = set(xs)" "9_999 in s"

toolkit.what: Profile a whole script: how many calls and how much time per function.
flags: sort by time including everything a function calls
sort by time spent in the function itself
save the results to open later (pstats, snakeviz)

toolkit.what: A sampling profiler that attaches to a running Python process without restarting it. The tool for "production is stuck at 100% CPU".
flags: print every thread's current stack (what is it doing right now?)
live view of the busiest functions

toolkit.what: Split any iterable into tuples of n (Python 3.12+). The standard way to send rows to an API or a database in chunks.
flags: tuples of up to 500; the last may be shorter
raise if the last batch is short (3.13+)

toolkit.what: Lazy building blocks. `groupby` only groups *neighbouring* equal keys, so sort by the same key first.
flags: runs of items with the same key
the first 10 items of any iterator
toolkit.example: for level, lines in groupby(sorted(log, key=level_of), key=level_of): ...

toolkit.what: Fold a sequence into one value. Reach for `sum`, `max`, `math.prod` or `"".join` first; use `reduce` only when none fits.
flags: always pass `initial`, or an empty list raises TypeError
toolkit.example: merged = reduce(lambda acc, d: acc | d, layers, {})

toolkit.what: A very fast linter that also fixes what it can: old-style idioms, unused imports, likely bugs.

steps.prompt: Match each option to what it does.
pairs: setup code that is not timed
save the profile to a file
show what a running process is doing now

code: from itertools import batched, groupby, islice
print([(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby(words, key=lambda w: w[0])])
steps.explain: `batched` yields tuples and the last one is short. The words are already sorted by first letter, so `groupby` finds three runs. `islice(it, 2, 5)` takes items at positions 2, 3 and 4.

steps.prompt: A report counts log lines per level with `groupby(lines, key=level_of)`, and `ERROR` appears three separate times in the output with different counts. Why?
options: `groupby` only groups neighbouring items; sort by the same key first, or use `Counter(map(level_of, lines))`
Log levels must be lowercase for `groupby`
steps.explain: `itertools.groupby` is not SQL GROUP BY: it starts a new group every time the key changes. For counting, `Counter` is simpler and does not need sorting.

steps.prompt: A worker in production has been at 100% CPU for an hour. You cannot restart it or add code. What do you run first?
options: `py-spy dump --pid <pid>` to see the stack it is stuck in, then `py-spy top` if it keeps moving
`python -m cProfile worker.py`, which profiles the running process
steps.explain: `cProfile` and `timeit` start a new process, so they cannot look inside one that is already running. `py-spy` reads the running interpreter's stacks from outside (on Linux it may need `sudo` or the right ptrace permission).

steps.prompt: Time one call in isolation, then profile the whole script sorted by cumulative time.
steps.explain: `timeit` is for one snippet; `cProfile` is for finding which function in a whole program takes the time.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before you optimise, profile: `cProfile -s cumtime` locally and `py-spy` in production show where the time really goes. After a change, prove it with `timeit`. Let `ruff check --fix` run in your editor and CI so idioms are never a review comment.
